title: From AI Tutors to AI Study Mates
author: Dr. Philippa Hardman
summary: Dr. Philippa Hardman summarizes and analyzes a major 2026 paper by Khosravi et al. that argues AI tools optimized for task completion -- including both default LLMs and AI tutors -- actively undermine durable learning by enabling what the paper calls 'metacognitive laziness.' The key evidence is a large Wharton/Penn randomized study of nearly 1,000 high school math students: the AI groups performed 48-127% better during practice, but the unguarded GPT group performed 17% worse than the control group on a subsequent exam when AI was taken away, confirming the 'learning-performance paradox' in which AI improves short-term performance while degrading long-term capability. The paper distinguishes between AI built for work (optimize output, minimize cognitive effort) and AI built for learning (introduce desirable difficulty, promote metacognition, build persistence), arguing that LLMs imported into education were designed for the wrong purpose. Hardman explains the paper's proposed solution -- 'AI study mates' or learning companions -- which differ from tutors by remembering what you've worked on, knowing where you got stuck, and pushing you toward the thinking you're avoiding, so that capability persists once the AI is gone. The article argues that all the "AI improved completion rates by 40%" pitches in circulation are measuring the wrong outcome: performance with AI present rather than learning that persists without it.
points: * The learning-performance paradox: AI tutors improve performance dramatically while the tool is present but cause learners to perform measurably worse on assessments after the tool is removed -- the gain was borrowed, not built. * Fan et al. (2024) documented 'metacognitive laziness': when AI is available, learners abdicate the planning, monitoring, and self-evaluation that make learning durable; the work gets done but the capability doesn't develop. * LLMs were built for work, not learning: the logic that makes them useful at work (optimize output, minimize cognitive effort, treat each interaction as disposable) is precisely what makes them unsuitable as learning tools. * The distinction between AI tutors (waits for questions and asks questions back regardless of what you actually need) and AI study mates (remembers your history, knows where you got stuck, pushes you toward avoided thinking) is the central design challenge for L&D professionals. * The meta-analyses showing LLMs improve assignment and performance scores are measuring the wrong thing -- performance with AI present rather than retention, transfer, and capability that persists when the tool is removed -- which makes them actively misleading for learning assessment.
quotes: Students were split into three groups: one had access to a standard ChatGPT-4 interface ('GPT Base'), one had access to a version with teacher-designed guardrails that gave hints rather than answers ('GPT Tutor'), and a control group had only textbook and notes. During the practice sessions, the AI groups crushed it. The GPT Base group performed a whopping 48% better than the control group.

Then, the researchers took the AI away and gave everyone an exam. The students who had used the unguarded GPT Base performed 17% worse on the exam than the control group who had never had AI access at all.
TLDR: AI tutors didn't help students to learn -- it helped them to perform.
AI tutors tend to be optimised for task completion and actively undermine the processes through which durable learning happens.

The LLMs entering education and training were not built for education or training -- they were built for work. The logic that makes them useful at work -- optimise the output, minimise cognitive effort, treat each interaction as disposable -- is precisely what makes them unsuitable as learning tools.

Yan, Greiff, Lodge and Gasevic (2025) put it bluntly in Nature Reviews Psychology: we're confusing performance gains with learning. In practice, this means every 'AI improved completion rates by 40%' pitch you've been getting this year is potentially measuring the exact outcome that doesn't matter.
An AI study mate remembers what you've worked on, knows where you got stuck, and pushes you toward the thinking you're avoiding -- resulting in capability that persists when the AI is gone.
